title: KiroCrew App Store editorial feed
description: How the store FEATURES apps: the Discover page's editorial layout. Each entry in `sections` is one BLOCK of the page -- a `form` saying how its contents are arranged, and the `items` it arranges -- so the grouping a reader sees is written down rather than inferred from array position. The category rail's order is a document of its own (`category-order.json`) because the two never reference each other -- an item names apps, never a category -- and because sharing a file would mean sharing a version gate, so a bump made here would re-sort every category on an older client. Only REFERENCES apps by name -- app data always resolves through the registry, so editorial can never inject a phantom or spoofed app. Read tolerantly: an unknown `form` skips its whole block, an unknown item `type` skips just that card, and anything that fails validation is dropped individually rather than failing the page.

schemaVersion.description:
Integer major. Additive-only within a major: new fields are optional and existing fields never change meaning. A major the client does not support triggers FULL fallback (cache -> bundled snapshot -> built-in heuristic), not a partial render.

ONE CARVE-OUT, and it is narrow: a `sections` VARIANT that has never appeared in a published document may be removed, or have its bounds tightened, without a major bump. Compatibility is a promise to consumers, and a variant no client can ever have read has none -- the CDN's own history is the evidence. It does not extend to a variant that shipped even once.

minClientVersion.description: Independent of the schema major. Lets the server force older clients onto their bundled default when a doc relies on behavior they lack. A client below this ignores the document entirely.

sections.description:
Ordered Discover layout. Each entry is one BLOCK of the page, and it declares its `form` -- how its contents are arranged relative to each other -- plus the `items` it arranges. A block is the unit the reader perceives: the page below is two blocks, not three cards, and saying so here is what stops the client inferring grouping from array position.

The forms are viewport-INDEPENDENT on purpose. `full`, `row` and `carousel` each have a meaning on a phone as well as a desktop -- a row still scrolls horizontally when it only shows one and a half cards. What must never appear here is a MEASURE: `two-column`, `3-up`, a pixel width or a card height cannot be honoured on a narrow viewport, so those stay in the client where the viewport is known. The curator authors relationships; the client resolves geometry.

appRef.description: Must resolve to a live, non-tombstoned entry in the merged registry. The publish pipeline enforces this; the client drops the reference if it does not resolve.

artwork.description:
Editorial artwork for an item, authored by the CURATOR and hosted by the catalog. Shared across every item variant on purpose: artwork is orthogonal to what an item contains, so a future variant inherits it without touching this definition. Raster only -- an SVG is a script host, and a regex screen over untrusted XML was defeated three separate ways.

TWO FORMS, ONE FIELD. Authored, `ref` is a path to a file in THIS repository (`art/spotlight-tasks.png`) -- the curator cannot know a digest that does not exist until publish runs. Published, the same key holds the content-addressed path the publish step emitted (`assets/editorial/<sha256>.png`), whose digest is covered by the document signature and is what gives a client end-to-end integrity for bytes carrying no signature of their own. The pattern below admits both because one schema validates both stages; `verify_dist` is what proves the published form is the addressed one.

ref.description: Light-appearance artwork. Required when `artwork` is present at all: a dark-only section would render nothing on the default appearance.

refDark.description: Optional dark-appearance variant. Absent means the light bytes are reused, which is why the light one is opaque by requirement.

alt.description: Accessible description. Absent is allowed and means the artwork is decorative -- the section's own title and blurb already name the content, so an empty alt is correct rather than lazy.

assetRef.description: A relative path, never an absolute URL and never a traversal: a curated feed must not be able to point the client's renderer at a third-party host, and the publish step must not be able to read outside the repository. Lowercase, single dots only, one extension.

section.description:
One block of the Discover page: a `form` and the `items` it arranges. Closed per known form here, but the CLIENT must skip an unrecognized `form` -- the whole block, items included -- rather than reject the document. Validating strictly is for the publish gate; the reader is deliberately more tolerant, and that tolerance is what lets a new form publish before every client can draw it.

WHY TWO LEVELS. `form` answers 'how are these arranged', `items[].type` answers 'what is each one'. Collapsing them into one enum is what the earlier single-level shape did, and it forced the client to infer arrangement from ARRAY POSITION -- the first entry rendered full-width, the next two side by side, with the grouping existing nowhere in the document. A curator who then added a fourth entry had no way to say which block it joined.

EXTENDING THIS. A new arrangement gets a new `form` value; a new kind of card gets a new `items[].type`. Never a sub-discriminator inside an existing variant: an unknown `form` or `type` is safe because it is skipped, whereas a flag inside a variant the client already recognises makes every older client render the new shape as a broken old one.

sectionFull.title: full -- one item across the whole width
sectionFull.description:
`items` holds EXACTLY one, and that is a property of the form rather than a limit imposed on it: two things that each occupy the full width can only stack, and stacked full-width blocks are two `full` sections. A bound of one here means the schema states the fact instead of leaving the client to enforce it.

This is the loudest placement on the page, which is also where a card carrying no artwork shows worst -- it renders as text alone in the slot most likely to be seen.

sectionRow.title: row -- items side by side, scrolling horizontally when they overflow
sectionRow.description:
For items meant to be COMPARED. The client lays them out across the available width and scrolls what does not fit; on a narrow viewport that is one and a half cards and a swipe, which is the same relationship expressed at a different size.

`minItems` is 2 for the same reason a `collection` needs two apps: one item has nothing to sit beside, and a row of one renders as a half-width card against empty space. A curator with a single item to feature wants `full`, which is a statement that it deserves the width.

`maxItems` is 6 because everything past the first screenful of a horizontal scroller is seen by almost nobody -- a cap the reader will not reach is a cap that silently discards curation.

sectionCarousel.title: carousel -- one item at a time, advanced by the reader
sectionCarousel.description:
For items that each deserve the full width and cannot share it. Unlike `row`, the reader sees one and navigates; the value is that the block's HEIGHT is fixed no matter how many items it holds, so a curator can add a fourth story without the page growing.

NO RENDERER SHIPS FOR THIS FORM YET. It is defined here so the vocabulary is settled, but a published `carousel` is skipped whole by every current client -- validated, signed, delivered, and invisible. Do not author one expecting it to appear; the client-side implementation is what makes this form real, and until then `row` and `full` are the two that draw.

`minItems` is 2 because a carousel of one is a `full` section with a control that does nothing.

item.description:
One card inside a section. `type` says what it contains; the enclosing section's `form` says how it is arranged with its siblings. The client must skip an unrecognized `type` and keep the rest of the section, which is a narrower failure than skipping the block: an unknown FORM means the arrangement cannot be drawn at all, an unknown TYPE means one card cannot.

A variant earns its place by having a SURFACE, not by being conceivable. A type with no renderer validates, publishes, and then silently vanishes into the reader's skip path, which looks exactly like a bug from the curator's side.

itemApp.title: app -- featured placement for ONE app
itemApp.description:
The app's own name is the heading, so there is no `title`: a curator who wants to say something other than the app's name is describing a collection of one, and a collection is the variant that carries a theme.

Separate from `collection` because the two differ in what they REQUIRE, not merely in how many apps they hold: a collection is meaningless without a theme, and this variant is meaningless with one. Expressing both as a single variant with a variable-length list forces `title` to be optional everywhere and pushes 'required when more than one' into code the schema cannot see.

blurb.description: Overrides the app's registry description for this placement only. Absent means the registry description is used, which is the normal case -- an override is for when the editorial angle differs from how the author describes their own app.

itemCollection.title: collection -- several apps under a curator's theme
itemCollection.description:
`title` is REQUIRED: the theme is the entire reason several unrelated apps appear together, and an untitled collection gives the reader no way to understand why these apps share a card.

`minItems` is 2 because a one-app collection is an `app` placement wearing a costume. `maxItems` is small because every member is RENDERED -- there is no collection detail page to hold an overflow, so a cap the card cannot draw would silently discard members that validated and published. Raising it requires giving the card somewhere to put them first.

title.description:
The curator's theme. Names why these apps belong together -- not a category name, which the taxonomy already covers.

Two INDEPENDENT assertions rather than one clever pattern. A title must contain a non-space character, because `minLength` counts BYTES while the client counts visible characters: a whitespace-only title passes the cross-document checks, publishes, and is then dropped by the client, so the card vanishes with no error at the gate and nothing in the client's log. It must also be ONE line, because HTML collapses a newline to a space, so a multi-line title would validate, sign, and render as something other than what was authored.

Both are written anchored, with `[\s\S]*` shoulders so they still mean CONTAINMENT. That spelling matters: `[\s\S]` matches every character including a line break, whereas the tempting `^\S+$` rejects every title containing a space and a bare `^[^\r\n]*\S[^\r\n]*$` still admits a trailing newline, because the Python validator this repository runs treats `$` as end-of-input OR just before a trailing `\n` (ECMA-262 does not). The second assertion is negated, so its inner pattern must stay a containment test -- anchoring it tightly would flip its meaning from `contains a line break` to `IS a line break` and let `"Theme\n"` through.

appRefs.description: Ordered. The card renders them in this sequence; there is no ranking, sorting or scoring applied on top, so the curator's order is what a reader sees.

blurb.description: One line under the title. Absent is fine when the title carries the idea on its own.
